statement: Ali has cards 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. He removes one, then splits the other four into two piles of two with equal totals. How many different cards could he have removed?

choices.misconception: I added all five cards, got 15, which is odd, and decided it can never be shared, but I forgot that one card is taken away first.
I found that taking away 5 works and stopped without checking the other cards.
I counted only the even cards, 2 and 4, because I thought even cards would make sharing work.
I forgot the two piles must have the same total, so I thought any card could be taken away.

hints: Two equal piles always make an even total.
Find the total of all five cards. Ask which cards leave an even total when taken away, then check that the four cards left really split into two equal pairs.
Taking away 2 or 4 leaves an odd total, which can never split into two equal piles. Now test taking away 1, 3 and 5.

solutions.reliable: Try each card. Take away 1: 2 + 5 = 3 + 4, works. Take away 2: the rest add to 13, odd, fails. Take away 3: 1 + 5 = 2 + 4, works. Take away 4: the rest add to 11, odd, fails. Take away 5: 1 + 4 = 2 + 3, works. So 3 different cards work: 1, 3 and 5. The idea to keep: before searching, use odd and even to throw out the cases that can never work.
solutions.elegant: Two equal piles make an even total, and 15 is odd, so the card taken away must be odd: 1, 3 or 5. A quick check shows each of these really does split into two equal pairs, so the answer is 3.

whyOnTest: Parity narrows a search: the total of two equal piles must be even, which rules out cards before any trying.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
